Everything the CLI does, a front end would do through\n * here - which is the point: one place makes the security decisions, so a second transport cannot\n * accidentally skip a check.\n *\n * <h2>The order of checks in {@link #signIn} <em>is</em> the security property</h2>\n * <ol>\n *   <li><b>Source label</b> first. An unusable label aborts the request before any lookup or\n *     derivation, so it is never a way to get work done for free and never a bucket to hide\n *     behind.</li>\n *   <li><b>Password policy</b> second. A candidate we refuse to hash is rejected <em>at a\n *     derivation's cost</em>, never cheaply - otherwise \"is this password long enough\" becomes an\n *     unauthenticated oracle.</li>\n *   <li><b>Penalty windows</b> third, keyed by the <em>canonical identifier</em> whether or not an\n *     account exists for it. This is what keeps our own limit from being weaponised (Rule 3): the\n *     per-account counter is global across sources, so spraying sources cannot lock a real user out\n *     of their own account; and because a blocked caller is refused <em>before</em> any lookup or\n *     write, it cannot extend its own penalty.</li>\n *   <li><b>Account lookup</b> fourth.</li>\n *   <li><b>Password verification</b> fifth.</li>\n *   <li><b>Account status</b> <em>after</em> verification. Reading {@code status} first would let an\n *     unauthenticated caller learn which accounts are administratively disabled - from the message\n *     and from the timing of the early return.</li>\n *   <li><b>Session issue</b> last.</li>\n * </ol>\n *\n * <h2>Equal work on every refusal (Rule 6)</h2>\n * Every branch that could separate \"this identifier exists\" from \"it does not\" pays roughly one\n * PBKDF2 derivation: unknown account, corrupt row, wrong password, and a candidate that fails\n * policy all do. {@link PasswordHasher#chargeDummy()} spends the work where there is nothing real to\n * verify. The throttled branch is the one deliberate exception, and it is not an oracle: the same\n * cheap refusal is reachable whether or not the identifier exists, since the bucket was created by\n * the earlier attempts either way. Charging the derivation there would defeat a limiter whose whole\n * purpose is to bound that cost. Each branch is timed separately in {@code EqualWorkTest}.\n *\n * <h2>What this class never does</h2>\n * It never logs, returns, or stores the plaintext password, the stored hash, the salt, or the\n * iteration count. It never echoes caller bytes back: every string it returns was re-read from the\n * database and re-validated. It never decides an outcome from a caller-supplied token, identifier\n * mapping, or role.\n */\npublic final class AuthApi implements AutoCloseable {\n\n    private final SqlIdentityStore store;\n    private final PasswordHasher hasher;\n    private final AuditLog audit;\n    private final Config config;\n    private final TimeSource time;\n    private final SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();\n\n    public AuthApi(SqlIdentityStore store, PasswordHasher hasher, AuditLog audit, Config config,\n                   TimeSource time) {\n        this.store = store;\n        this.hasher = hasher;\n        this.audit = audit;\n        this.config = config;\n        this.time = time;\n    }\n\n    // ------------------------------------------------------------------ registration\n\n    /**\n     * Registers an account.\n     *\n     * @param passwordChars consumed and erased on every path, including the rejected ones\n     * @param sourceLabel   asserted origin; see {@link SourceId} for why it is treated as hostile\n     */\n    public AuthResult register(String emailRaw, String usernameRaw, char[] passwordChars, String sourceLabel)\n            throws IdentityStoreException {\n        // Validation first, before any secret is touched. from the caller, from time, from a sequence, or from the account\n * it belongs to, so tokens are neither predictable nor correlatable. There is no {@code of(String)}\n * that fabricates a token from caller-supplied structure; {@link #parse} accepts a submitted string\n * only as an opaque handle to look up, and only after checking its shape.\n *\n * <h2>What the database holds</h2>\n * Not this string. {@link #tokenHash()} is a SHA-256 digest, and the digest is the primary key of\n * the session row. A read of the {@code session} table - through a backup, a stolen file, or an\n * SQL-injection hole elsewhere in the product - therefore does not hand over live credentials:\n * the digest is not invertible and is what the server compares against. This is the same reason\n * a password database stores a hash rather than the password, applied to bearer tokens.\n *\n * <h2>Remaining risk, stated plainly</h2>\n * A bearer token is still a bearer token: whoever holds the 43 characters holds the session until\n * it expires or is revoked. Hashing protects the stored copy, not the copy in the caller's hand.\n * Mitigations in this code: short TTL (configuration-bounded at 24 h, default 15 min), absolute\n * per-account session cap, explicit revocation that also fires on a password change, and no\n * binding claim beyond the token itself - see README \"Limitations\" for what a real deployment adds\n * (TLS, per-Principal binding, and cookie attributes via {@link CookieSpec}).\n */\npublic record SessionToken(String value) {\n\n    static final int TOKEN_BYTES = 32;\n    static final int TOKEN_CHARS = 43; */\n    @Override\n    public boolean equals(Object o) {\n        return o instanceof SessionToken other\n                && public int hashCode() {\n        // Not secret-dependent: derived from the value but intentionally not the value itself.\n        return value.hashCode();\n    }\n\n    private static boolean isTokenChar(char c) {\n        return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || (c >= '0' && c <= '9')\n                || c == '-' || c == '_';\n    }\n\n    private static byte[] Everything the CLI does, a front end would do through\n * here - which is the point: one place makes the security decisions, so a second transport cannot\n * accidentally skip a check.\n *\n * <h2>The order of checks in {@link #signIn} <em>is</em> the security property</h2>\n * <ol>\n *   <li><b>Source label</b> first. An unusable label aborts the request before any lookup or\n *     derivation, so it is never a way to get work done for free and never a bucket to hide\n *     behind.</li>\n *   <li><b>Password policy</b> second. A candidate we refuse to hash is rejected <em>at a\n *     derivation's cost</em>, never cheaply - otherwise \"is this password long enough\" becomes an\n *     unauthenticated oracle.</li>\n *   <li><b>Penalty windows</b> third, keyed by the <em>canonical identifier</em> whether or not an\n *     account exists for it. This is what keeps our own limit from being weaponised (Rule 3): the\n *     per-account counter is global across sources, so spraying sources cannot lock a real user out\n *     of their own account; and because a blocked caller is refused <em>before</em> any lookup or\n *     write, it cannot extend its own penalty.</li>\n *   <li><b>Account lookup</b> fourth.</li>\n *   <li><b>Password verification</b> fifth.</li>\n *   <li><b>Account status</b> <em>after</em> verification. Reading {@code status} first would let an\n *     unauthenticated caller learn which accounts are administratively disabled - from the message\n *     and from the timing of the early return.</li>\n *   <li><b>Session issue</b> last.</li>\n * </ol>\n *\n * <h2>Equal work on every refusal (Rule 6)</h2>\n * Every branch that could separate \"this identifier exists\" from \"it does not\" pays roughly one\n * PBKDF2 derivation: unknown account, corrupt row, wrong password, and a candidate that fails\n * policy all do. {@link PasswordHasher#chargeDummy()} spends the work where there is nothing real to\n * verify. The throttled branch is the one deliberate exception, and it is not an oracle: the same\n * cheap refusal is reachable whether or not the identifier exists, since the bucket was created by\n * the earlier attempts either way. Charging the derivation there would defeat a limiter whose whole\n * purpose is to bound that cost. Each branch is timed separately in {@code EqualWorkTest}.\n *\n * <h2>What this class never does</h2>\n * It never logs, returns, or stores the plaintext password, the stored hash, the salt, or the\n * iteration count. It never echoes caller bytes back: every string it returns was re-read from the\n * database and re-validated. It never decides an outcome from a caller-supplied token, identifier\n * mapping, or role.\n */\npublic final class AuthApi implements AutoCloseable {\n\n    private final SqlIdentityStore store;\n    private final PasswordHasher hasher;\n    private final AuditLog audit;\n    private final Config config;\n    private final TimeSource time;\n    private final SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();\n\n    public AuthApi(SqlIdentityStore store, PasswordHasher hasher, AuditLog audit, Config config,\n                   TimeSource time) {\n        this.store = store;\n        this.hasher = hasher;\n        this.audit = audit;\n        this.config = config;\n        this.time = time;\n    }\n\n    // ------------------------------------------------------------------ registration\n\n    /**\n     * Registers an account.\n     *\n     * @param passwordChars consumed and erased on every path, including the rejected ones\n     * @param sourceLabel   asserted origin; see {@link SourceId} for why it is treated as hostile\n     */\n    public AuthResult register(String emailRaw, String usernameRaw, char[] passwordChars, String sourceLabel)\n            throws IdentityStoreException {\n        // Validation first, before any secret is touched. These outcomes are about the caller's own\n        // input and may be specific, because none of them says whether an account exists.\n        SourceId source = SourceId.parse(sourceLabel);\n        if (source == null) {\n            Password.erase(passwordChars);\n            audit.append(Reason.INVALID_REQUEST, null);\n            return AuthResult.of(Reason.INVALID_REQUEST);\n        }\n        Identity email = Identity.parseClientEmail(emailRaw);\n        if (email == null) {\n            Password.erase(passwordChars);\n            audit.append(Reason.INVALID_EMAIL, null);\n            return AuthResult.of(Reason.INVALID_EMAIL);\n        }\n        Identity username = Identity.parseClientUsername(usernameRaw);\n        if (username == null) {\n            Password.erase(passwordChars);\n            audit.append(Reason.INVALID_USERNAME, null);\n            return AuthResult.of(Reason.INVALID_USERNAME);\n        }\n        Password password = Password.adopt(passwordChars); // erases the array if it is rejected\n        if (password == null) {\n            audit.append(Reason.INVALID_PASSWORD, username);\n            return AuthResult.of(Reason.INVALID_PASSWORD);\n        }\n\n        try {\n            String hash = hasher.hash(password); // closes the password\n            // Budgets and the account cap are enforced inside the store's transaction, behind the\n            // serialisation row, so neither can be raced.\n            SqlIdentityStore.Outcome outcome =\n                    store.register(username.canonical(), username, email, email.canonical(), hash, source);\n            // The audit gets the store's specific fact; the caller gets the collapsed one.\n            audit.append(outcome.reason(), username);\n            return AuthResult.of(outcome.callerReason());\n        } catch (IdentityStoreException e) {\n            password.close();\n            audit.append(e.reason(), username);\n            throw e;\n        }\n    }\n\n    // ------------------------------------------------------------------ sign-in\n\n    /**\n     * Verifies a credential and, on success, issues a session.\n     *\n     * @param passwordChars consumed and erased on every path\n     */\n    public AuthResult signIn(String identifierRaw, char[] passwordChars, String sourceLabel)\n            throws IdentityStoreException {\n        long now = time.nowEpochSeconds();\n\n        SourceId source = SourceId.parse(sourceLabel);\n        if (source == null) {\n            Password.erase(passwordChars);\n            audit.append(Reason.INVALID_REQUEST, null);\n            return AuthResult.of(Reason.INVALID_REQUEST);\n        }\n\n        Identity identifier = parseIdentifier(identifierRaw);\n        Password password = Password.adopt(passwordChars);\n        try {\n            // (2) Policy. Refused at verification cost, so password policy is not an oracle.\n            if (password == null) {\n                chargeEqualWork();\n                if (identifier != null) {\n                    chargeBothBuckets(source, identifier, now);\n                }\n                audit.append(Reason.INVALID_PASSWORD, identifier);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // A malformed identifier never reaches the database. Equal cost, same message.\n            if (identifier == null) {\n                chargeEqualWork();\n                audit.append(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL, null);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // (3) Penalties, before any read or write.\n            boolean sourceBlocked =\n                    store.isPenaltyActive(SqlIdentityStore.bucketKindSource(), source.canonical(), now);\n            boolean accountBlocked =\n                    store.isPenaltyActive(SqlIdentityStore.bucketKindAccount(), identifier.canonical(), now);\n            if (sourceBlocked || accountBlocked) {\n                audit.append(Reason.THROTTLED, identifier);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // (4) Lookup. A row that fails strict re-validation is a storage fact, not a user fact:\n            // it becomes the same outcome as \"no such account\".\n            SqlIdentityStore.Account account;\n            try {\n                account = store.findByCanonicalIdentity(identifier);\n            } catch (IdentityStoreException corrupt) {\n                chargeEqualWork();\n                audit.appendEvent(AuditEvent.ROW_REJECTED_AS_ABSENT);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            if (account == null) {\n                chargeEqualWork();\n                chargeBothBuckets(source, identifier, now);\n                audit.append(Reason.ABSENT_ACCOUNT, identifier);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // (5) Verify. A stored credential that fails strict decoding is the same user-visible\n            // outcome as \"no such account\": matchesStored already charged the equal-work dummy\n            // before throwing, so this branch also costs a derivation. Only a genuine cryptographic\n            // failure propagates - there the service truly cannot decide, and it must not guess.\n            boolean ok;\n            try {\n                ok = hasher.matchesStored(password.chars(), account.passwordHash());\n            } catch (IdentityStoreException corrupt) {\n                if (corrupt.reason() != Reason.CORRUPT_RECORD) {\n                    throw corrupt;\n                }\n                chargeBothBuckets(source, identifier, now);\n                audit.appendEvent(AuditEvent.ROW_REJECTED_AS_ABSENT);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n            if (!ok) {\n                chargeBothBuckets(source, identifier, now);\n                audit.append(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL, identifier);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // (6) Status, only now that the credential is proven.\n            if (!\"active\".equals(account.status())) {\n                store.clearBucket(SqlIdentityStore.bucketKindAccount(), identifier.canonical());\n                // The audit gets the specific fact; the caller's AuthResult carries the same reason\n                // every other sign-in refusal carries. Handing back ACCOUNT_DISABLED here would make\n                // the audit log uniform while leaving the distinction one getter call away from a\n                // front end - and a front end that shows, returns in a header, or branches on it\n                // reopens the exact oracle this ordering exists to close.\n                audit.append(Reason.ACCOUNT_DISABLED, identifier);\n                return AuthResult.of(Reason.BAD_CREDENTIAL);\n            }\n\n            // Verified: reset the per-account counter. The per-source counter is deliberately left\n            // alone - clearing it on success would let an attacker who knows one real credential\n            // keep their source bucket permanently empty by alternating a correct login with a\n            // thousand guesses.\n            store.clearBucket(SqlIdentityStore.bucketKindAccount(), identifier.canonical());\n\n            // (7) Transparent cost upgrade, while the candidate is still in hand. Re-encoding is a\n            // credential change, so outstanding sessions are revoked with it: a token stolen before\n            // the upgrade cannot outlive it.\n            if (hasher.needsRehash(account.passwordHash())) {\n                try {\n                    Password forRehash = Password.copyOf(password.chars());\n                    if (forRehash != null) {\n                        store.replacePasswordHash(account.id(), hasher.hash(forRehash));\n                        store.revokeAllSessions(account.id());\n                        audit.appendEvent(AuditEvent.CREDENTIAL_REENCODED);\n                    }\n                } catch (IdentityStoreException e) {\n                    // The user did authenticate. Rate limiting's job is to bound guesses per window. If, during a penalty, we still verify a candidate that turns out correct, we've leaked... what? The check \"does this guess work while blocked\" requires a full verification — which is exactly the CPU cost the limiter bounds. Per-account one-in-flight means concurrent legitimate logins from the same user (e.g., a browser double-submit, or a burst) get refused. In this test's case, 8 parallel logins with the correct password for the same account: 1 succeeds, 7 shed.\n\nHmm. Is \"one in-flight decision per account\" too aggressive? Consider: the security property I need is that the *limit can't be exceeded by K sockets*. The overshoot is what matters: with a per-account claim, overshoot = 0. Without it, overshoot = K-1.\n\nAlternative that preserves legitimate concurrency: allow up to N (say 2) in flight per account. That bounds the overshoot to 1 rather than 0. The right move is to decide deliberately which behaviour is correct, and update the test to document the new invariant with a clear reason.\n\nActually, let me think harder about correctness for legitimate users. Is refusing concurrent sign-ins on the same account acceptable? For a real service: two devices signing in simultaneously for the same account is plausible but rare, and the refusal is transient (the caller can retry in a moment) — but the user-visible message here is the generic bad-credential message, which is misleading (\"wrong password\" when it isn't). That's a UX/correctness concern: Rule 6 requires identical messages for failures, so I can't distinguish \"try again\". But is a *false refusal of a correct credential* acceptable? Under the pre-existing design, the same thing happens whenever a penalty is live: the correct password is refused (Rule 3 tension). Now it happens under contention too.\n\nI think there's a cleaner framing.
